featured_image.name: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures sink as Iran conflict escalates

items.description:
The war between the United States, Israel, and Iran has sent shockwaves through global energy and financial markets, with crude oil prices surging and investors scrambling for safe-haven assets as the conflict enters its fourth day with no sign of de-escalation.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, spiked as much as 13% over the weekend before settling with gains of roughly 9% on Monday, climbing into the upper $70s per barrel. The surge came as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint through which roughly 20% of the world's daily oil supply passes. Tanker traffic through the strait dropped to near zero, with more than 150 ships anchoring outside to avoid the risks.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Oil tops $82 as Iran conflict threatens Strait of Hormuz

featured_image.name: Oil prices rise sharply after US, Israeli attacks on Iran

items.description:
Oil prices surged to their highest levels since early 2025 this week as an expanding military conflict between the United States and Israel on one side and Iran on the other rattled global energy markets and raised fears of prolonged supply disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude closed Monday's session up roughly 6.7%, after earlier spiking as much as 13% to above $82 per barrel — its highest point since January 2025, according to Reuters. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude also climbed more than 6% on Monday. By Tuesday, prices continued to rise, with Brent topping $82 a barrel as concerns mounted over the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.[1][2]

items.title: IAEA confirms damage at Iran's Natanz nuclear site

featured_image.name: Iran's Natanz nuclear site hit: Tehran vows to rebuild ...

items.description:
The International Atomic Energy Agency confirmed on Tuesday that entrance buildings at Iran's underground Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant sustained damage during the ongoing U.S.-Israeli military campaign, but said no radiological consequences are expected.

"Based on the latest available satellite imagery, IAEA can now confirm some recent damage to entrance buildings of Iran's underground Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant (FEP)," the agency wrote on X. "No radiological consequence expected and no additional impact detected at FEP itself, which was severely damaged in the June conflict."[1]

featured_image.name: Oil prices surge, but no panic yet, as Iran war continues - NPR

items.description:
The U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran, now entering its fourth day, has sent shockwaves through global energy and financial markets, with oil prices surging, the Strait of Hormuz effectively shut to commercial shipping, and investors scrambling for safe-haven assets.

Brent crude spiked as much as 13% over the weekend before settling around $79 per barrel on Monday, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude jumped roughly 8%. Analysts at Barclays and Rystad Energy have warned that prices could reach $100 a barrel if disruptions persist. On Tuesday in Asia, oil prices continued climbing, with Brent adding another $1.10 to near $79.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: India cuts industrial gas supply after Qatar halts LNG production

featured_image.name: Qatar suspended liquefied natural gas (LNG) production on ...

items.description:
Indian energy companies on Tuesday slashed natural gas deliveries to industrial consumers by 10 to 30 percent after Qatar — the country's largest supplier of liquefied natural gas — halted all LNG production following Iranian drone strikes on two major facilities.[1][2]

Petronet LNG, India's top LNG importer, notified GAIL, the leading gas marketing firm, and other companies of reduced supplies late Monday, according to Reuters, citing four industry sources. GAIL and Indian Oil Corporation then relayed the cuts to their downstream customers.[2][3][1]

items.title: Trump won't rule out ground troops in Iran as strikes enter third day

featured_image.name: Donald Trump won't rule out boots on ground in Iran

items.description:
President Donald Trump on Monday declined to rule out deploying American ground forces to Iran, telling the New York Post he would send them "if necessary" as U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran continued into their third day under Operation Epic Fury.[1]

"I don't have the yips with respect to boots on the ground — like every president says, 'There will be no boots on the ground.' I don't say it," Trump told the Post. "I say 'probably don't need them,' [or] 'if they were necessary.'"[2][1]

At the Pentagon, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth struck a similar tone during the first detailed briefing since the operation began on Saturday, refusing to specify what the administration would or would not do. "President Trump ensures that our enemies understand we'll go as far as we need to go to advance American interests," Hegseth said, appearing alongside Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine.[3][4]

items.title: Six US troops killed as Trump won't rule out ground forces in Iran

featured_image.name: War in the Mideast widens as Trump says strikes on Iran ...

items.description:
The United States is "not currently postured" to send ground forces into Iran, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Monday, even as President Donald Trump refused to take the option off the table and the American military campaign entered its third day with mounting casualties on both sides.[1][2]

Rubio, speaking on Capitol Hill before briefing the congressional "Gang of Eight," said the administration is confident its objectives can be achieved through air and naval power alone. But in comments to the New York Post, Trump struck a different tone: "Probably don't need them," he said of ground troops, adding, "if they were necessary" — a stark departure from the traditional presidential assurance of "no boots on the ground."[3][4]
